title: Huawei found guilty of stealing trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
content: Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US. In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage. Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation. Huawei said the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests". Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions. However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise. Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada. Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors. During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge. "For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement . "Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable." However, defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff. Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge. "The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said. "Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board." Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal. "If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

title: Households braced for soaring energy bills with new price cap to be announced
content: Domestic energy bills are expected to soar in January for millions of households, with regulator Ofgem to announce the precise increase shortly. A typical annual bill is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, in a forecast made ahead of the official announcement. Ofgem's new cap, which sets a maximum price for each unit of energy, will come into force at the coldest time of year. Customers pay for what they use and charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support. The government will make a £100 payment to millions of households to help cover winter costs, in addition to an ongoing VAT cut on electricity. The warm home discount will also take £150 off bills for six million households on benefits this winter. There have been calls for this support, funded through everyone's bill, to be extended. "We are staring down the barrel of a brutal winter," said Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice. "Every day our advisers see people whose budgets have been completely wiped out by years of compounding crises. Millions of households are entering the coldest months of the year with nothing left." About 20 million households in England, Scotland and Wales are on variable energy tariffs set by Ofgem's price cap. Those on fixed tariffs will be unaffected, but the impact may be felt when that tariff expires and the replacement is more expensive. If forecasts prove correct, then a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity and paying by direct debit will see a bill rise of about £37 a month from January to the end of March. If sustained for a year, it would mean the typical annual bill will rise by £443 to £2,166 compared with the current cap. However, individual usage differs, so for every £100 spent on energy now, the new cost is likely to be about £126. Wholesale gas prices are the dominant driver of the forecast higher prices. The war in Iran has led to higher international gas prices. With storage levels relatively low ahead of the winter, suppliers had to buy ahead at steeply higher prices. The average price of gas is 166% higher than late last year, before the Iran war began, according to suppliers' trade body Energy UK. Andrew Sissons, from research foundation Nesta, said that the expected change in bills for households could have a wider impact. "Higher energy bills will reduce household spending on everything else, which will have a knock-on effect across the rest of the economy," he said. On Sunday, Chris O'Shea, the boss of British Gas owner Centrica, told the BBC he was "hugely concerned" about the impact of the January rise in prices. There was a "massive problem" with people not paying their bills in the UK, he said, with some unable to pay, and an "increasing number of people that are choosing not to pay their bills". Energy UK calculations suggest that £67 of the average annual energy bill covers the cost of this debt. Those who pay their bill every three months, rather than by monthly direct debit, face the biggest addition. Total energy debt was likely to rise towards £7bn by the end of the year, the trade body said. Predictions suggest domestic energy prices could stay high throughout next year. Even if wholesale gas prices were to fall, then network costs for running and upgrading the electricity system are expected to be high. The government has temporarily cut 5% VAT from electricity bills until the end of June next year, which is expected to save the typical household about £45 a year. The £100 support payment will be made, automatically, to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with equivalent payments in Scotland and Wales. But Citizens Advice said that those on prepayment meters in particular, who often top up the most during the coldest months, would see the money disappear quickly. It said it was bracing for a wave of more people seeking emergency help this winter, because they could not top up their meters
